## The idea

A dominant chord makes a particular future chord feel likely: its tonic, a
fifth below. A *secondary dominant* directs that expectation toward one of the
other diatonic chords in the home key. For a moment, the target receives the
kind of emphasis normally reserved for the tonic. The progression can then
continue without abandoning its original key.

In C major, G is the dominant and D major is the dominant of G. The F-sharp in
D major lies outside the C-major scale and has a theoretical tendency to rise
by semitone to G when the chords are voiced to realise that motion. The label
V/V means "dominant of the dominant."
The slash names the chord being approached; it does not by itself announce that
the entire key has changed.

Use controlled comparison to isolate the changed chord. Place D minor, the
ordinary diatonic ii chord, before G. Then raise its F to F-sharp, creating D
major, while leaving rhythm, voicing, and synth alone. One changed pitch is
enough to alter the force of arrival.

## Run this

The first four-chord statement stays within C major. In the second, a single
quality value changes D minor into D major. Roots and qualities remain visible
as data, so the chromatic intervention can be read as readily as it can be
heard.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72
use_synth :piano

diatonic = [
  {root: :c3, quality: :major},
  {root: :d3, quality: :minor},
  {root: :g2, quality: :major},
  {root: :c3, quality: :major}
]

tonicised = [
  {root: :c3, quality: :major},
  {root: :d3, quality: :major}, # V/V: F-sharp points toward G
  {root: :g2, quality: :major},
  {root: :c3, quality: :major}
]

define :play_progression do |chords|
  chords.each do |item|
    play_chord chord(item[:root], item[:quality]),
      release: 1.8,
      amp: 0.75
    sleep 2
  end
end

play_progression diatonic
sleep 2
play_progression tonicised
```

D minor supplies a diatonic route to G. D major introduces F-sharp and makes the
dominant relation to the following G explicit in the chord data.
The root-position chords in this program do not place F-sharp next to a higher G
in one voice, so they demonstrate harmonic preparation rather than the specific
semitone resolution. Both versions arrive on the same chord; listen for whether
the altered path makes that arrival feel more strongly prepared.

## Change one thing

1. Change the target G major to G minor in both arrays. D major still points
   toward a root a fifth below, but the B-flat at resolution changes the colour
   of the arrival. Listen for what the dominant relation preserves and what the
   target quality changes.
2. Restore G major and make the D chord `:dom7`. The added C forms a tritone
   with F-sharp and introduces another tendency tone. Compare the greater
   urgency of the seventh chord with the plainer D-major triad.
3. Move D major away from G so that D minor intervenes before the expected
   target. The chromatic pitches are unchanged, but their promised arrival is
   delayed or denied. Hear how a chord that was directional can begin to sound
   unexplained when its context no longer answers it.

## Why it works

The home key supplies a family of diatonic chords. A secondary dominant borrows
the dominant-to-tonic relation and applies it locally to one member of that
family. Choose the target root, move a perfect fifth above it, and construct a
major triad or dominant seventh. Because the new chord is being built relative
to the target rather than the home scale, it often contains at least one
chromatic pitch.

This emphasis is called *tonicisation* when it remains local. The target is
brightly prepared, but subsequent chords continue to support the home tonic. A
modulation lasts long enough for the ear to adopt a new tonic and reinterpret
later scale degrees around it. The presence of an outside pitch cannot decide
between the two. What follows the chromatic chord, and for how long, supplies
the stronger evidence.

Slash notation resembles a nested address. V/V first identifies V as the
temporary target, then asks for V in relation to that target. Code can resolve
the address in the same two stages: find the target root in the current key,
move seven semitones above it, then build the major or dominant-seventh quality
that creates the pull.

Voice leading can make that calculation perceptible. In C major, F-sharp often
rises to G while the other D-major notes find nearby positions in the G chord.
The root-position renderer above does not realise that line; a nearest-voicing
renderer would be needed to compare it directly. If F-sharp is hidden in a
distant octave or directed downward, the written V/V remains present while one
of its clearest melodic cues is weakened.

## Take it further

Write an eight-bar diatonic progression in a major key. Choose one diatonic
chord other than I and precede it with that chord's dominant. Keep original and
tonicised versions in parallel data arrays and render them consecutively with
the same rhythm, voicing, and synth. Label the temporary target, slash numeral,
and every chromatic pitch. The altered version should produce one clearly
prepared local arrival, followed by enough unchanged harmony to confirm that
the original key still governs the passage.
